name: Wobenzym

lead: Wobenzym is a tablet combining proteolytic enzymes, typically trypsin and bromelain, with the flavonoid rutin. People use it to reduce swelling and bruising and to speed recovery, which in appearance terms means a shorter swollen period after procedures such as eyelid surgery and a faster return to training.
Trials have tested it after blepharoplasty, in lymphedema, in knee osteoarthritis and after exhausting exercise.

paras: It is taken orally as enteric-coated tablets, commonly around surgery or after hard exercise, according to the maker's labelling. Ingredients vary by country.
Reported effects are mostly mild gastrointestinal symptoms and occasional rash. Labels advise caution with bleeding disorders, anticoagulants, pregnancy and ulcers.

chain: Faster-looking healing and quicker return to training
angle.text: People take Wobenzym around cosmetic surgery to reduce swelling and bruising and after hard exercise to recover. Quicker recovery means a sooner final look and more training.

lead: Wobenzym is an enteric-coated oral enzyme preparation made by Mucos Pharma of Germany, combining trypsin from pig pancreas, bromelain from pineapple stem and rutin; some regional versions add papain and chymotrypsin.[1] It was developed in the 1950s by Max Wolf and colleagues under the idea of 'systemic enzyme therapy'.[1]

In appearance terms it is used to reduce post-operative swelling and bruising, helping the face return to its final shape sooner, and by athletes for recovery, which supports more training. A randomised trial in 20 patients compared it with antiedema and hemostyptic drugs after upper eyelid blepharoplasty.[2]
In Germany and parts of Europe it is approved as a drug for joint pain and swelling; in the US it is sold as a dietary supplement.[1]
infobox: Drug in parts of Europe; supplement in US[1]

paras: A tablet is described as containing trypsin, bromelain and rutin, with papain and chymotrypsin in some regional versions.[1] Mucos later became part of Atrium Innovations and then Nestle Health Science, although sources give differing dates.[1]

In a randomised study of 20 blepharoplasty patients, oral proteases (Wobenzym) were compared with another oedema and haemostatic regimen for haematoma, oedema and pain, and no undesirable side effects were observed.[2]

Wobenzym has also been tested on scar healing: a prospective cohort of 60 women compared Caesarean scar outcomes with and without systemic enzymotherapy.[3] A randomised trial in healthy active adults examined it after exhaustive eccentric exercise.[4]

A randomised trial of 55 women with arm lymphoedema after mastectomy compared Wobenzym with diuretics; after 7 weeks arm volume, circumference and skinfold thickness improved significantly more with Wobenzym, with more patients pain-free.[5]

In a double-blind trial of 80 patients with acute knee osteoarthritis, Wobenzym and diclofenac gave no significant difference in pain improvement; adverse events were mainly gastrointestinal.[6] A 2015 randomised placebo-controlled trial in knee osteoarthritis has also been published.[7]

Adverse events reported in the diclofenac comparison included constipation, vomiting, bloating, one allergic rash and dizziness.[6] Grokipedia lists cautions for bleeding disorders, anticoagulant use, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and ulcers; it also notes the FDA has cited unapproved disease claims on enzyme products.[1]

timeline.event: Systemic enzyme therapy developed by Max Wolf and colleagues.[1]
